senses: a cognomen of several celebrated Romans in the
la:noun:Cato.html:
Căto, ōnis, m.
1. catus
,
a cognomen of several celebrated Romans in the gens Porcia, Valeria, Vettia al.
M. Porcius Cato the elder, distinguished as a rigid judge of morals; hence with the appel. Censorius; whose most celebrated works were the Origines and De Re Rustica,; sqq.; ; ; cf., concerning him, Bernhardy, Röm. Litt. p. 521 sq.; 650; Bähr, Lit. Gesch. p. 515; 258; 354 al.; Ellendt, p. xix.-xxv.—As appel. of a severe judge,, prooem. fin.; .—Hence,
Cătōnĭānus, a, um, adj., of Cato: familia,: aetas,: illa (i. e. praecepta),: lingua,i. e. of high morality,.—
His descendant, M. Porcius Cato the younger, the enemy of Cœsar, who committed suicide after the battle of Pharsalia, at Utica; hence with the appel. Uticensis.—
Cătōnīni, ōrum, m., the adherents or friends of Cato, ; cf. catonium.—Concerning both, and the Porcian family in gen., v. Hertz, p. 19 Bip.—On account of their serious and austere character, serious, or gloomy, morose men are called Catones, ; cf. ; ; .—
Valerius Cato, a celebrated grammarian of Gaul, and poet of the time of Sulla, ; ; ; ; .—
Dionysius Cato, author of the Disticha de moribus, prob. about the time of Constantine; v. the Disticha, with the Sententiae of Syrus, at the end of the Fabulae of Phaedrus, Bip.

la:adj:catus.html:
cătus, a, um, adj.
root ka-; Sanscr. ça-, to whet, sharpen; cf. cos, cautes, cuneus; Sabine, = acutus, acc. to Bip.
. *
Sharp to the hearing, clear-sounding, shrill (cf. acutus, 2.): jam cata signa fere sonitum dare voce parabant, Enn. ap. Varr. l. l. (Ann. 447 Vahl.). —
Transf. to intellectual objects, in a good and bad sense.
In a good sense, clear-sighted, intelligent, sagacious, wise, opp. stultus (in prose probably never naturalized; hence Cic., in prose, adds ut ita dicam; v.the foll.): catus Aelius Sextus, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 335 Vahl.); ; ; Don. and Ruhnk.; : prudens et, ut ita dicam, catus,.—Constr. with inf.: jaculari,.—With gen.: legum,.—Of abstract things: dicta, Vahl.: consilium,.—
In a bad sense, sly, crafty, cunning, artful ( = callidus, astutus): cata est et callida,; so ; ; ; .—Adv.: cătē, conform. to II. A.: sapienter, docte et cordate et cate,; ; .—Comp. and sup. not in use in the adj. or in the adv.

la:noun:catus.html:
cătus, i, m.,
a male cat (post-class.), ; scanned, cātus, Poët. ap. Anth. Lat. 5, p. 162, 3 al.

căterva, ae, f.,
a crowd, troop, a bandof men; in the sing. and plur. (class. in prose and poet.; syn.: turba, manus, agmen).
In gen.: comitum,; cf. ; ; ; : Postumius obviam cum bene magnā catervā suā venit,; so ; cf. : catervae testium,: contra dicentium,: pugilum,: infernae,— Poet., of animals: pecudum,: avium,flocks,: canum,: anguinea,.—
Trop.: verborum. a farrago of words, .—
Esp.
In milit. lang. freq., a body of soldiers, a troop, company, band; esp. of the loose order of barbarian nations (opp. to the Roman legions); cf. ; ; so ; ; ; ; 12, 33; ; ; ; —Of foot-soldiers (opp. equites), ; ; .—Rare of Roman troops, Petr. poët. 124, 281; or of cavalry,.—
In dramatic lang., the whole company or troop of actors (usu. called grex). fin.; and perh. also id. Cas. fin.; cf. Cic. de. Or 3, 50, 196; . 118.

la:noun:catena.html:
cătēna, ae, f. (once with
num. distrib. as piur. tantum: trinis catenis vinctus,) [Sanscr. kat, to fall away; cf. catax].
A wooden bracket, brace, etc., for holding two beams together, ; ; .—
A chain,
Used as a fetter, shackle, etc.; usu. in plur. (syn. vincula): catenis vincire aliquem,; : catenas indere alicui,: in catenas conicere aliquem,; : catenas inicere alicui,: in catenis aliquem Romam mittere,: in catenis aliquem per urbem ducere,: eximere se ex catenis,: rumpere catenas,: catenas alicui exsolvere,—In sing., ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Of a chain stopping the entrance of a harbor: catena ferrea valde robusta,.—
Trop., a constraint, fetter, barrier, bond: taetra belua, constricta legum sacratarum catenis,: compesce animum frenis, catenā,: validā teneamur catenā,; : splendidiore nunc eos catenā sed multo graviore vinctos esse, quam cum, etc.,: qui ad superiora progressus est.. laxam catenam trahit nondum liber,; .—
A chain of gold or silver worn by women as an ornament, ; .—
A series of things connected together, a chain, series, (but , is a false reading for quod armis; v. Lachm.).—
Trop.: (praecepta oratoria) in catenas ligare,.
